Article Title: The healing hands of Indian cricket: How Rajeev Kumar and his village gave 50 masseurs to Indian cricket
Article Text:

A journey worth celebrating

Rajeev Kumar with KL Rahul (Special Arrangement)

In 2002, when Rajeev Kumar arrived in Delhi, his only goal was to earn a stable income. Armed with a diploma in massage therapy from Jodhpur University, he took up his first job, earning just Rs 100 a month. Nearly a quarter of a century later, he has travelled the world alongside some of the greatest cricketers of his generation. But the journey was anything but easy. Before becoming one of Indian cricket's most trusted support staff members, Rajeev spent years travelling in crowded Delhi buses, walking miles to save money and wondering if his dream would ever become a reality."When I first came to Delhi, everything felt overwhelming," Rajeev tells TimesofIndia.com from Southampton, where he is working with Southern Brave."I travelled by bus, walked long distances and struggled for three to four years. At that time, I never imagined I would one day work with the Indian cricket team and travel the world."Those early years tested every ounce of his resolve.He did not have a mobile phone. Someone eventually bought him a Nokia 1100 because he could not afford one himself. His first earning was just Rs 100. Stable work remained elusive for almost five years but he refused to give up.Dr Choudhary introduced him to Ashish Nehra in 2004, who used to come to a clinic in Greater Kailash for his massage sessions. It opened the doors to the Delhi District Cricket Association (DDCA) for Rajeev, who then spent nearly a decade with Delhi's Ranji Trophy team, quietly earning a reputation for his work ethic and professionalism.When the Indian Premier League (IPL) was launched in 2008, he joined the Delhi Daredevils from the inaugural season. Assignments in the ISL, Pro Kabaddi and hockey followed before the biggest break of his career arrived in 2016, when he became part of the Indian team during the T20 World Cup.What had once seemed impossible had become reality. Today, Rajeev measures success differently."Around 50 boys and girls from my village have entered this profession," he says proudly. "Some work in the IPL, some with Ranji teams, some in the Indian team, while others are in yoga and Ayurveda."For someone who once struggled to establish himself, becoming an inspiration back home means more than any medal."When people from my village meet me and say they are proud, it feels wonderful. They ask me to help more youngsters enter this profession. If I can create opportunities for them, it is a blessing."If Rajeev credits one cricketer for transforming his career, it is Ashish Nehra.Their association began while Nehra was recovering from injuries. Rajeev would spend hours treating the left-arm pacer, often on the terrace of his house because Nehra preferred sessions under the sun."When he returned to the Indian team, he never forgot me," Rajeev says. "During the 2009 IPL in South Africa, he helped me get opportunities and later recommended me for other assignments. I will always be grateful."That loyalty became the foundation of a career that eventually took him into the Indian dressing room. It was Nehra who introduced Rajeev to former India captain MS Dhoni in 2015 and in a year's time, Rajeev was in the Indian men's team dressing room.Over the next eight years, Rajeev worked alongside four Indian captains and witnessed some of the defining moments of modern Indian cricket. Each leader left a different impression.MS Dhoni's calmness immediately eased his nerves as a newcomer. The former captain regularly invited him for breakfast or dinner and ensured every member of the support staff felt valued."My first day bhai checked on me. He said: 'Tension mat lena Rajeev bhai. Bilkul chill hoke kaam karo. Kisi bhi tarah ki jaroorat ho mera kamra khula hai.' Mahi bhai took me out for dinner that day," he recalls.Virat Kohli impressed him with an obsession that bordered on relentless."I have known Virat since his Delhi days," Rajeev says. "His transformation has been unbelievable. He completely changed his lifestyle and inspired everyone around him."He still remembers Kohli playing through personal grief after the death of his father, a memory that continues to define the batter's mental strength in Rajeev's eyes."What a knock he played that day. All of us in that dressing room knew that we are witnessing something special, and it was just starting of a great career," he says."Under Virat, the Indian team's fitness went a notch above. He pushed everyone. For him fitness was everything. He was relentless. He worked so hard. I was surprised when he turned vegan, because the Virat I know used to love his food. I just want to tip my hat to the great man. What he did for Indian cricket is something that I can't explain in words," he adds.Then came Rohit Sharma , whose leadership style revolved around empathy."He speaks to every member of the support staff, asks about our families and always makes everyone feel included. Even in this year's IPL, he met and the first question he asked was about my family."Then came the young captain Shubman Gill , whose majestic form helped India draw the five-match Test series in England in 2025. It was also Rajeev's last series with the Indian team."Very sweet boy with a very good head on his shoulder. He has got the best of Mahi bhai, Virat, and Rohit. He has only shown glimpses of his excellent leadership skills. He will take Indian cricket to greater heights," says Rajeev.For Rajeev, those qualities mattered as much as tactical acumen.Life inside the Indian dressing room was built on relationships that extended beyond the boundary rope.During the Covid-19 pandemic, Rajeev's younger son fell seriously ill. What followed remains one of the most emotional chapters of his career."The entire Indian team stood by me," he says. "The players kept calling to ask about my family and even offered financial support. I can never forget that."Those gestures reinforced what he already believed about the group he served for years.Rajeev experienced cricket's cruelest moments from the closest quarters. He remembers the devastation after India's semifinal exit in the 2016 T20 World Cup. But nothing matched the silence inside the dressing room after the 2023 ODI World Cup final in Ahmedabad."Everyone was emotional. It was my first stint with the team and I felt so bad.(Everyone was so down) " he recalls."Then that night in Ahmedabad. Agar mera bas chale toh mai November 19 ko hata do (I want to eradicate memories of November 19). The dressing room was heartbroken."Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit after the defeat, he says, offered words of encouragement when the squad needed them most.As South Africa closed in during the final of the 2024 T20 World Cup, Rajeev admits he could do little except pray."When they needed around 30 runs towards the end, I was sitting quietly near the boundary praying for a miracle.(Please god not again)."The miracle arrived. India became world champions."For me, it felt like years of hard work had finally been rewarded."Away from the spotlight, the dressing room had its lighter moments too.Mohammed Siraj, Mohammed Shami and Kuldeep Yadav were among the regular visitors seeking treatment, but Kuldeep stood out."We used to joke that Kuldeep deserved an award because he probably took the most massages," Rajeev says with a laugh.His bond with Rishabh Pant was equally special. When Pant had his horrific car accident, Rajeev rushed to a Hanuman temple with his family to pray."Looking at the accident, we feared the worst," he says. "Thankfully, he recovered. He is a wonderful person who always helps others."Rajeev Kumar 's story is not merely about working alongside cricket's biggest stars.It is about a young man from a small village who arrived in Delhi with almost nothing, endured years of uncertainty, embraced education when sports science was still finding its feet in Indian cricket, and quietly became one of the most trusted figures behind the scenes.His hands helped players recover, but his own journey was built on resilience, humility and gratitude.From earning Rs 100 to celebrating a World Cup triumph on the biggest stage, Rajeev Kumar's greatest achievement may not be the medals he collected along the way. It is proving that even the quietest journeys can leave the loudest impact.
Article Summary: Rajeev Kumar is a former India men's team masseur. He worked with MS Dhoni, Virat Kohli, Rishabh Pant and Rohit Sharma. Rajeev spent years travelling in crowded Delhi buses, walking miles to save money. His first earning was just Rs 100 a month.

Article Title: Yash Thakur's untold story: Karate, rejections, father's dream and India's newest pace hope
Article Text:
Yash Thakur (BCCI Photo)

A reward for patience



From Karate to Cricket



'Dhoni ke jaise keeper banna hai'



The transformation



A father's dream



The emotional call



The debut



NEW DELHI: Zimbabwe has become India's preferred destination to bring in young talent. Just like in 2024, when Abhishek Sharma, Dhruv Jurel, Riyan Parag, Sai Sudharsan and Tushar Deshpande received their maiden India caps, this year's tour also saw Ashok Sharma and Yash Thakur make their T20I debuts. The series also marked the return of Mayank Yadav after a long injury layoff.Ahead of the tour, the spotlight was firmly on Mayank and Ashok, both known to consistently bowling over 150 kmph. Thakur, however, was hardly part of the conversation. The Vidarbha pacer had quietly gone about his business, staying away from the hype surrounding India's new generation of fast bowlers.Why Yash Thakur?Among the current crop of young pacers featuring Mayank, Ashok and Gurnoor Brar, who was fast-tracked into the Indian side, Thakur's inclusion surprised many.Zimbabwe has long been India's platform to test young cricketers. It is where youngsters get opportunities to prove themselves, and those who perform often strengthen their claim for a permanent place in the side. This time, Thakur grabbed that opportunity with both hands.Despite receiving far less attention than many of the cricketer, he quietly continued doing the hard work.Thakur began the series on the bench as Ashok was preferred for the opening T20I.But when his long-awaited opportunity came in the second match, he made an immediate impact.The 27-year-old pacer, who had hardly been spoken about before the tour, surprised many by clocking 140 kmph with his very first delivery in international cricket.He consistently bowled hard lengths and back-of-a-length deliveries to return figures of 4-0-30-2 on debut. He retained his place for the third and final T20I and impressed once again, finishing with figures of 4-0-45-2.At 27, Thakur had to wait much longer than most to wear the India jersey. His biggest strength was his single-minded focus. He never allowed rejection to affect him and remained patient despite repeatedly being overlooked. He always believed his opportunity would arrive one day.When it finally did, he made sure he made the most of it.Thakur, who was part of India's victorious 2016 ACC Under-19 Asia Cup squad and picked up nine wickets during the tournament, also faced plenty of disappointments before finally earning his India cap at the age of 27.He missed out on the Under-19 World Cup. He was never considered a prodigy or fast-tracked into the senior side. Instead, he kept working hard and steadily built his career through domestic cricket.He made his List A debut for Vidarbha in 2017 before making his first-class and T20 debuts over the next two seasons.His domestic breakthrough came in the 2021-22 Vijay Hazare Trophy, where he finished as the tournament's highest wicket-taker with 18 wickets in seven matches. He also played a key role in Vidarbha's Irani Cup triumph in 2025.While his parents worried about the setbacks, Thakur never lost sight of his goal.That's his story."Under 16 ka competion tha. He didn't get a single mtch in the tournametn. As a parent we all were upset and were talking about why is he not taking chance despite being in top form. But when he came, we asked him, he silently went inside the room saying 'mai aur mehnat karunga'. Such is the person he is. He is very calm and silently he waited for his opportunity. May be this quality in his has got him the reward," Yash's mother Kajal Thakur told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview."Rejections mili usko but wo mehnat karna rha. Bhagwaan kuch achha socha tha uske liye. This is just a beginning for him I know. He is a guy who keeps his head down and keeps working hard. I am so proud of him," the mother said.Before making a name as a fast bowler for India and in the IPL, Thakur's sporting journey could have taken a completely different path.His father, Ravi Singh Thakur, was a state-level Karate champion and wanted his son to follow in his footsteps. Thakur did well in the sport too, winning medals at junior-level competitions. But his mother, Kajal, was never comfortable seeing her son compete in a combat sport. Like most mothers, she constantly worried about injuries. Eventually, her concerns led Yash away from Karate and towards cricket."In one tournament happened in Solapur. He kicked his opponent on his nose during a match and he started bleeding. That really worried me. What if Yash would have been at that kid's place. I had to argue with his father multiple times and somehow I managed to take Yash away from Karate," he said.While his parents debated his future, Yash had already made up his mind.He wanted to become a cricketer.From the terrace of his house, he would spend hours watching children train at a nearby cricket academy. He watched batters play big shots, bowlers celebrate wickets and wicketkeepers dive behind the stumps. Every day, he stood there imagining himself on that ground.The day he finally quit Karate, he went straight to his father with one request: "mujhe wo academy join karwa do, cricket khelunga."That decision changed his life.Soon, Yash joined the Praveen Hinganikar Cricket Academy (PHCA) in Nagpur, where he came under the guidance of coach Praveen Hinganikar."Mai puch usse kya banna chahte ho.. he replied Dhoni ki tarah wicketkeeper batter," Hinganikar recalled.Yash was just 10 years old when he joined the academy. For the first few months, he trained only as a wicketkeeper.Then came one practice session that completely altered the course of his career."There were no bowlers in the nets. I asked him to bowl. The moment I saw him bowling, I told him, 'Abb keeping gloves nahi pehenna hai, you start bowling'," Hinganikar recalled.The decision was difficult for the young Yash to accept."He was upset for almost a month because he wanted to be a wicketkeeper. But his father stood firmly behind me. He told Yash, 'Whatever Praveen Sir says, you have to do it.' That support made all the difference," the coach said.Coach Hinganikar quickly realised that Thakur had something special in his bowling action. But before he could become a genuine fast bowler, there was one major challenge - his fitness.The youngster was overweight, and the first step was to transform his body.Rigorous fitness sessions, long-distance running, sprint drills and a strict diet became part of his daily routine. Only after improving his fitness did the focus shift completely to his run-up and bowling. Under trainer Prashant's guidance, Thakur underwent a remarkable transformation, shedding the extra weight within a year.By the age of 14, the chubby youngster had turned into a fit and athletic fast bowler."He is totally different from everyone. He has his own class. He can bowl six yorkers in an over," Hinganikar said."Now he has lost fat, he has all the muscles over bones. He is more stronger now. You ask him to bowl 7-8 overs on the trot, he can do that easily. He looks like he might not be intemedidating to the batters, but looks are deceptibve. He is a wonderful bowler. He can deceive batters with his slower ones and slow yorkers and yorkers too," the coach said.Standing behind Thakur throughout his journey was his father, Ravi Singh Thakur.From dropping him at the academy and picking him up after practice to managing his diet and buying cricket equipment, Ravi did everything possible to help his son chase his dream.But he had a dream of his own too — to one day see his son play for India.That dream finally came true when the 27-year-old made his India debut against Zimbabwe. The Vidarbha pacer featured in two T20Is and picked up four wickets in his first international assignment.Sadly, the man who had dreamt of that moment was not there to witness it.His father passed away after suffering a cardiac arrest in 2023.Today, Thakur has fulfilled his father's dream, while his mother continues to live that dream through her son.Before leaving for the Zimbabwe tour, Thakur had told TimesofIndia.com:"Ye papa ka hi dream tha. Aur main unke liye bahut grateful hoon kyunki day one se jab tak woh the, he always supported me and dekhna chahte the mujhe India jersey mein. Aaj wo hote to bahot khush hote [t was my father's dream. I am very grateful to him because from day one, until he was with us, he always supported me. If he were here today, he would have been extremely happy]."After returning from the India A tour of Sri Lanka, Thakur landed at Nagpur airport when he received the call informing him of his India selection.The first person he called was his mother."I was numb over phone when he called me and gave the news of his debut. He kept saying hello! hello! over phone, but I couldn't speak. When he came home from Sri Lanka, I just hugged him. He folded his hands in front of his father's photo and went inside his room," the mother said.She also remembered how determined her husband had been to see Yash wear the India jersey."Inke father mein joonoon tha sports ko leke. Wo khud Karate karte they. isko bhi banana chahte they. Jab cricket mein shift hua to wo ye kehte they ki jo mai nkhud nahi kar paya country ke liye, mai chanta hun Yash kare wo ek din - India khele," she said.A day before his debut, Yash called his mother with a simple message."Mummy, kal aap dekhna mere match."Those few words were enough to leave her emotional.The next day, she sat in front of the television, watching her son receive his India cap before claiming his first international wicket.At that moment, she looked at her husband's photograph and quietly said:"Dekho, ab aapka bachcha aaj India cap wear kar gaya hai.""Maine kisi ko nahi bulaya tha. I was alone and started watchign the match. Bas khushi ke aansu they. Kaash wo hote, to aaj bahot khush hote. Some people came they said, why I didn't go to Zimbabwe to watch, I said pehla match hai. Aage bahot mauke ayenge," the mother said.
Article Summary: Vidarbha pacer Yash Thakur made his India T20I debut against Zimbabwe. The 27-year-old bowled 140 kmph with his very first delivery in international cricket. He was part of India's victorious 2016 ACC Under-19 Asia Cup squad.

Article Title: From corn-husk pit to CWG glory: Sarvesh Kushare's journey to historic high jump silver
Article Text:
Sarvesh Kushare (Image credit: X)

From a corn-husk landing pit in Deogaon to India’s best-ever CWG men’s high jump finish, national record-holder Sarvesh Kushare finally has the big-stage medal he had long sought.Deogaon, a village near Nashik, is a long way from athletics’ biggest stages. Kushare, however, has long believed he belongs among the elite. On Monday night in Glasgow, he finally had the medal to prove it.Kushare became the first Indian to win a silver medal in the men’s high jump at the Commonwealth Games after clearing 2.25m. Jamaica’s Romaine Beckford also cleared 2.25m but took gold on countback, having sailed over the height on his first attempt. Kushare needed all three attempts. Neither could clear 2.28m.The Indian was in his element, smiling confidently and displaying a touch of showmanship before each attempt.Before his final try at 2.28m, he looked towards the crowd, smiled and put a finger to his lips, gesturing for silence. He could not clear the bar but celebrated the hardearned silver in style. “I got silver at 2.25m, but that is not even my best jump. I know I can jump higher, but yesterday was not the day. The weather conditions were not very conducive for any of us,” Kushare, who is supported by Olympic Gold Quest, told TOI .The national record-holder, who began training in his village on a makeshift landing pit filled with corn husks, said the silver provided the validation he had been seeking for a long time. “I have been participating at big-ticket tournaments — I have been to the Olympics, the World Championships, the Diamond League — but I didn’t win a medal there. I know that I belong to the big league, but it was not a good feeling to come back without a medal. I’m happy this has changed in Glasgow. Now I know that I can do better,” the Army athlete said.At the Paris Olympics in 2024, Kushare finished 13th in Group B and joint 25th overall after clearing 2.15m. At the World Championships in Tokyo last year, he became the first Indian men’s high jumper to reach the final and finished joint sixth with a then personalbest clearance of 2.28m.He has since raised the bar further. Kushare cleared 2.31m in Bhubaneswar last month to break Tejaswin Shankar’s eight-year-old national record of 2.29m and become the first Indian high jumper to breach the 2.30m mark. Kushare believes the CWG medal will spur him to work harder and make him mentally stronger for the challenges ahead.In Monday’s final, teammate Tejaswin was forced to withdraw after one unsuccessful attempt at 2.05m when a knee problem flared up. The Birmingham 2022 bronze medallist, however, remained beside the pit and guided Kushare until the competition ended.“We share a very good bond. I felt bad when he had to retire, but that was the right decision as continuing would have aggravated the pain. He has always been helping me, and it was no different yesterday,” Kushare said.
Article Summary: Sarvesh Kushare became the first Indian to win a silver medal in the men’s high jump at the Commonwealth Games after clearing 2.25m. The national record-holder, who began training in his village on a makeshift landing pit filled with corn husks, said the silver provided the validation he had been seeking for a long time.

Article Title: 'My mother was a little upset': India's CWG silver medallist Harjinder Kaur reveals emotional call after Glasgow success
Article Text:
Harjinder Kaur (IANS Photo)

Indian weightlifter Harjinder Kaur dedicated her Commonwealth Games 2026 silver medal to her mother, revealing that she always calls her first after winning a major event.Harjinder won silver in the women's 69kg category with a combined lift of 227kg (101kg snatch and 126kg clean and jerk), earning her second straight Commonwealth Games medal after winning bronze in Birmingham in 2022."I usually call my mother first whenever I win a medal, and today was no different; I spoke to her briefly right after my event as she was a little upset with me for being away at competitions for so long," Harjinder told news agency IANS.The 29-year-old stayed in medal contention throughout the competition and secured second place with a successful 126kg clean and jerk in her final attempt. Although she admitted she has lifted heavier weights in training, she was pleased with her consistency."I am happy with my silver medal. I have achieved better clean and jerk lifts during my training, but I am satisfied that all six of my lifts were valid," she said.Harjinder also revealed that improving on her previous Commonwealth Games result was one of her biggest goals."I came here with the goal of changing the colour of my medal," she added.Harjinder's sporting career did not begin in weightlifting. She was initially a Kabaddi player and regularly cycled five kilometres to attend training sessions.It was only in 2016, at the age of 20, while studying at Punjabi University in Patiala, that she switched to weightlifting, a decision that has now helped her become a Commonwealth Games silver medallist.
Article Summary: Harjinder Kaur won silver in the women's 69kg category with a combined lift of 227kg. It was her second straight Commonwealth Games medal after winning bronze in Birmingham in 2022. The 29-year-old stayed in medal contention throughout the competition.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Priya Ghanghas, Preeti Pawar and Jadumani Singh assure India of boxing medals in Glasgow
Article Text:
Priya Ghanghas and Preeti Pawar (Image credit: X)

Preeti dominates to reach first CWG semifinal



Jadumani keeps India's medal hopes alive



Parveen and Kapil crash out



NEW DELHI: Priya Ghanghas (60kg) produced a stunning comeback to beat home favourite Niamh Mitchell, while Preeti Pawar and Jadumani Singh also reached the semifinals to assure India of at least three bronze medals at the Commonwealth Games boxing competition on Tuesday. However, Parveen Hooda and Kapil Pokhariya bowed out after losing their quarterfinal bouts.Reigning Asian Games champion Priya overcame a slow start to defeat Scotland's Niamh Mitchell 4-1 in a thrilling quarterfinal. The 20-year-old from Haryana had to battle not only her opponent but also a loud home crowd cheering every Scottish punch.Priya lost the opening round as four of the five judges gave it to Mitchell. But she made a strong comeback in the second round by attacking aggressively and forcing the Scottish boxer onto the back foot. Both boxers were penalised in the second round. Priya was warned for repeatedly lowering her head, while Mitchell lost a point for excessive clinching.Priya continued her attacking approach in the final round, landed the cleaner punches and sealed the contest by split decision. The judges scored the bout 28-27, 28-27, 27-28, 28-27 and 29-26 in favour of the Indian.Asian Games bronze medallist Preeti Pawar (54kg) produced a one-sided performance to beat Northern Ireland's Nicole Clyde 5-0. The Indian boxer had trained with Clyde during India's preparation camp in Belfast before the Games but looked far superior in the ring.Despite giving away height, Preeti controlled the fight with her speed, movement and accurate punching. She repeatedly broke through Clyde's defence with sharp combinations and comfortably won every round.The victory guarantees Preeti the first Commonwealth Games medal of her career. She will face Zambia's Catherine Mwape in the semifinals.Jadumani Singh (55kg) also secured at least a bronze medal after beating Zambia's Mwengo Mwale by unanimous decision.The Manipuri boxer dominated the contest from start to finish with smart movement, accurate counter-punching and clean combinations. He controlled the pace throughout and earned a comfortable 5-0 victory to move into the semifinals.India suffered two setbacks in the quarterfinals.Parveen Hooda (65kg) lost a close 2-3 decision to England's Sacha Hickey, while Kapil Pokhariya (90kg) was beaten by Scotland's Robert McNulty, ending both their Commonwealth Games campaigns.
Article Summary: Priya Ghanghas beats Scotland's Niamh Mitchell 4-1 in quarterfinal. Preeti Pawar beats Northern Ireland's Nicole Clyde 5-0. Jadumani Singh beats Zambia's Mwengo Mwale by unanimous decision. Parveen Hooda and Kapil Pokhariya lose in quarterfinals.

Article Title: From Taekwondo to two-time CWG medallist: Bindyarani Devi's inspiring journey
Article Text:
Bindyarani (right) with her taekwondo coach during her childhood days and (pic right) after winning bronze in Glasgow on Monday (Credit: TOI/IANS)

Coach A. Ranjan Singh couldn’t have been happier after his long-time student Bindyarani Devi clinched her second consecutive Commonwealth Games medal in Glasgow on Monday night. After winning silver in the women’s 55kg category at Birmingham Commonwealth Games in 2022, Bindyarani claimed bronze in the new 58kg division in Glasgow.Speaking about his former pupil, the veteran coach looked back to the day Bindyarani first walked into the weightlifting hall after beginning her sporting journey in taekwondo.“Her taekwondo coach felt she was a bit too small for the sport, so she shifted to weightlifting and started training with me. After one or two years, she began improving steadily,” Ranjan told TOI. “She had a naturally strong physique. Once she learnt the right techniques, she developed into a very good lifter.”But the coach, who trained her for nearly seven years at SAI, also had to rein in her eagerness to progress too quickly. “She wanted to lift heavier weights as soon as possible. But I told her that first she had to become technically sound. If you rush, there is a higher risk of injury, and an injury can end a career. We developed her slowly and systematically,” he said.It is perhaps one of the main reasons that Bindyarani has remained free of any major injury in her career.Ranjan was also quick to credit her discipline. “As coaches, we can only guide athletes. If they are sincere and train regularly, we can help them improve. If they are not disciplined, there is very little we can do,” he said.Bindyarani’s sincerity and discipline have indeed been the hallmarks of a career built on consistency. The 27-year-old, however, was not entirely satisfied with her performance on Monday. She looked disappointed after failing in her third clean and jerk attempt at 116kg. She eventually finished with a 199kg total (87kg snatch and 112kg clean and jerk) to secure the bronze medal. A successful final lift would have taken her total to 203kg, though it would not have altered the medal positions.“It wasn’t my best. I couldn’t perform the way I wanted to. But still, I’m happy that I could win a medal for India,” said Bindyarani. “It was quite difficult because I had to gain weight. I had to change a lot in my training and diet. It wasn’t easy, but I worked hard for it.”Moving up from 55kg to the 58kg category meant not only gaining body weight but also adapting her training and nutrition while maintaining her strength and explosiveness. Her family, however, never doubted that she would return home with a medal despite the shift in weight category. Their confidence stemmed from watching her overcome challenges from an early age.“My mother was crying like a baby. My father, my sisters, almost everyone in the family cried. But they were tears of happiness,” said her brother, Suraj Sorokhaibam.Long before she became an international weightlifter, Bindyarani also made her mark in the traditional Yaoshang Sports Festival in Manipur, where people compete in athletics, football, tug of war and other indigenous games held over five days.While celebrations continue at her home in Manipur, Bindyarani’s focus has already shifted to Asian Games . Beyond that lies her ultimate ambition, representing India at the Olympics.“I feel I haven’t achieved everything yet. There is still a lot more I want to do,” said the 27-year-old, who also broke Mirabai Chanu ’s national snatch record in the women’s 55kg category with an 88kg lift at the National Games in Dehradun, further cementing her place among India’s finest weightlifters. With Asian Games on the horizon and the Los Angeles Olympics firmly in her sights, Bindyarani’s pursuit of bigger milestones is far from over.
Article Summary: Bindyarani Devi won bronze in the women's 58kg category in Glasgow. The 27-year- old won silver in the 55kg category at Birmingham Commonwealth Games in 2022. Coach A. Ranjan Singh has been her coach for nearly seven years at SAI. The Manipur-born weightlifter is now targeting the Asian Games.

Article Title: Ajaya Babu wins silver in 79kg weightlifting after record-breaking duel at Commonwealth Games
Article Text:
Erry Hidayat Muhammad of Malaysia with his gold medal alongside Valluri Ajaya Babu of India with his silver medal, left, and Chris Murray of England with his bronze medal, right. (AP)

Fast-rising Indian weightlifter Valluri Ajaya Babu won the silver medal in the men's 79kg category at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, adding another medal to India's tally in the sport.The 21-year-old from Vizianagaram district in Andhra Pradesh lifted a Commonwealth Games record 149kg in the snatch and 181kg in the clean and jerk for a total of 330kg. He finished just one kilogram behind Malaysia's Erry Hidayat Muhammad, who won the gold with a Games record total of 331kg (147kg snatch + 184kg clean and jerk).England's Chris Murray claimed the bronze medal with a total lift of 325kg.The battle for gold went down to the final lifts in the clean and jerk. Hidayat first lifted 181kg to set a new Commonwealth Games record. Ajaya Babu then matched and bettered that effort by lifting 181kg in his final attempt, taking his total to 330kg. Hidayat responded with a successful lift of 184kg in his last attempt to regain the record and secure the gold medal.Earlier in the snatch, Ajaya Babu recovered after failing his second attempt at 149kg. He lifted the same weight in his third and final attempt to set a new Commonwealth Games record and finish first in the snatch standings ahead of Chris Murray (148kg) and Erry Hidayat Muhammad (147kg).Ajaya Babu opened the competition with a successful lift of 145kg in the snatch before finishing the section with the record lift.The silver medal was India's sixth medal in weightlifting at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.Ajaya Babu has been among India's top weightlifters in recent years. At the 2025 Commonwealth Championships in Ahmedabad, he won gold in the men's 79kg category with a personal-best total of 335kg (152kg snatch + 183kg clean and jerk), setting new championship records. That performance earned him direct qualification for the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.At the 2024 Commonwealth Championships in Suva, Fiji, he won gold medals in both the junior and senior men's 81kg categories.He also competed at the 2025 World Championships in Forde, Norway, where he finished 16th overall in a field of 39 lifters.
Article Summary: Valluri Ajaya Babu won the silver medal in the men's 79kg category at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The 21-year-old from Vizianagaram district in Andhra Pradesh lifted a Commonwealth Games record 149kg in the snatch. He finished just one kilogram behind Malaysia's Erry Hidayat Muhammad who won the gold with a Games record total of 331kg.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Indian boxers unfazed by baggage snag on arrival
Article Text:
Santiago Nieva (Image credit: X)

India’s boxing contingent arrived in Glasgow confident after a productive two-week multinational training camp in Belfast, but its final preparations were briefly disrupted when some boxers’ luggage failed to arrive ahead of Thursday’s opening ceremony.The 14-member squad travelled from Belfast to Glasgow on Tuesday after completing the intensive camp, during which the boxers benefitted from quality sparring and competition-specific training. However, several athletes were left without their bags, which also contained their ceremonial outfits, TOI has learnt.Sources said officials from the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) and the chef-de-mission’s office were at the airport on Wednesday, coordinating with the airline to ensure the baggage reached the contingent before the ceremony. The boxing competition begins on Friday and runs until Aug 1.The incident, however, has not gone down well with the Boxing Federation of India (BFI). Sources said that after the issue surfaced, the federation asked the boxers to submit declarations stating that they would not speak to the media about internal team matters and would instead remain focused on their performances.Despite the logistical hiccup, the mood in the camp remains upbeat. “We are settling in well in Glasgow. We had a good camp in Belfast where everybody got quality sparring and proper preparations. The boxers are managing their weights well. We will have the draws soon. We are coming with high expectations for this competition,” India women’s head coach Santiago Nieva told TOI .India’s 14-member squad features Olympic bronze medallist Lovlina Borgohain and Jaismine Lamboria, the world No. 1 in the women’s 57kg category.
Article Summary: India’s boxing contingent arrived in Glasgow confident after a productive two- week multinational training camp in Belfast. The 14-member squad travelled from Belfast to Glasgow on Tuesday after completing the intensive camp. Several athletes were left without their bags, which also contained their ceremonial outfits, TOI has learnt.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Gulveer Singh creates history, becomes first Indian to win Men's 10,000m medal
Article Text:
Gulveer Singh, of India, crosses the finish line to win the silver medal in the men's 10,000 meters final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, Tuesday, July 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Eranga Jayawardena)

Gulveer executes perfect race strategy



Historic milestone for Indian athletics



Indian long-distance runner Gulveer Singh scripted history by becoming the first Indian ever to win a medal in the men's 10,000m at the Commonwealth Games after claiming a memorable silver medal at the 2026 edition in Glasgow on Tuesday.The national record holder clocked 27:49.78 to finish second behind Australia's Ky Robinson, who took home the gold medal. David Mullarkey of the Isle of Man completed the podium with bronze, while traditional distance-running powerhouses Kenya and Uganda were surprisingly shut out of the medals.Competing in challenging rain-soaked conditions, Gulveer adopted a composed and tactical approach throughout the race. He remained comfortably within the leading pack for most of the 25-lap contest, conserving energy while closely tracking the frontrunners. With one lap remaining, the Indian runner was positioned in third place before producing a stunning burst of speed in the closing stages. His powerful finishing kick carried him into second place, securing a historic silver and one of India's greatest achievements in Commonwealth Games distance running.Gulveer's podium finish ended India's long-standing wait for success in the men's 10,000m at the Commonwealth Games. No Indian athlete had previously won a medal in the event, making his silver a landmark moment for Indian athletics.India's medallists so far are Mirabai Chanu (gold, weightlifting), Sharmila Dhankar (gold, women's shot put F57), Rishikanta Singh (silver, weightlifting), Muthupandi Raja (silver, weightlifting), Gyaneshwari Yadav (silver, weightlifting), Sarvesh Kushare (silver, men's high jump), Gulveer Singh (silver, men's 10,000m), Harjinder Kaur (silver, weightlifting), Valluri Ajaya Babu (silver, weightlifting), Bindyarani Devi (bronze, weightlifting), Shilpa K. Shyla (bronze, women's shot put F57) and Jhandu Kumar (bronze, para powerlifting).
Article Summary: Gulveer Singh becomes first Indian ever to win a medal in the men's 10,000m at the Commonwealth Games. The national record holder clocked 27:49.78 to finish second behind Australia's Ky Robinson, who took home the gold medal. David Mullarkey of the Isle of Man completed the podium with bronze.

Article Title: Lopes Cabral's curling goal against Argentina voted FIFA World Cup's best goal
Article Text:
Cape Verde's Sidny Lopes Cabral, celebrates scoring his side's second goal against Argentina during the World Cup round of 32 football match in Miami Gardens, Fla., Friday, July 3, 2026. (AP Photo)

Cape Verde added another chapter to its World Cup journey on Monday after Sidny Lopes Cabral won the public vote for the Goal of the Tournament.Lopes Cabral earned the honour for his curling strike into the top corner against Argentina during the 2026 FIFA World Cup . The goal came in extra time of Cape Verde's Round of 32 match in Miami Gardens, drawing his side level at 2-2 against the defending champions. Argentina, however, went on to win the match 3-2.The 2026 edition marked Cape Verde's first appearance at the FIFA World Cup. The African side progressed from the group stage before exiting in the Round of 32 against Argentina.Lopes Cabral's effort was voted the best among the 308 goals scored during the tournament. It finished ahead of Eldor Shomurodov's lob for Uzbekistan against Congo and Wilson Isidor's rising strike for Haiti against Morocco.FIFA shortlisted 12 goals for the public vote, which closed on Monday.Lopes Cabral's celebration also became one of the memorable moments of the tournament. After scoring, he broke away from teammates, climbed into the stands to hug his girlfriend and then searched for his mother.“Before the game, I’d told my mom and my girlfriend that if I scored, I’d run over to them,” he said. “When I got there, I saw my mom crying. She hadn’t even realized I was right there. Everyone was busy tending to her because she had fainted when I scored.”Their campaign began with a 0-0 draw against eventual champions Spain, with goalkeeper Vozinha playing a key role in the result.
Article Summary: Cape Verde's Sidny Lopes Cabral won the public vote for the Goal of the Tournament. His curling strike against Argentina during the 2026 FIFA World Cup was voted the best among the 308 goals scored during the tournament. The goal came in extra time, drawing his side level at 2-2 against the defending champions.

Article Title: Commonwealth Games: IOA issues health advisory amid Glasgow chill
Article Text:
Indian contingent pose as they arrive for the opening ceremony of the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games (PTI Photo)

New Delhi :

With Glasgow hit by a sudden spell of cold, cloudy and rain-soaked weather, the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) and the country’s chef-de-mission office have advised athletes to take preventive measures to minimise the risk of upper respiratory and airborne infections during the Commonwealth Games.Sources told TOI that athletes have been verbally briefed at their respective hotels, with officials urging them to avoid unnecessary outdoor exposure, dress warmly and wear face masks while travelling or in crowded indoor spaces. Frequent hand washing has also been recommended as an added precaution.The advisory comes after temperatures dropped sharply over the past two days, making conditions considerably colder, especially during the evenings. A few Indian athletes have reported mild cold symptoms, including runny noses, but none has required hospitalisation.Officials stressed there is no cause for alarm, while underlining the importance of preventive care with several medal events still to come. “It is quite cold and cloudy here,” Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra said, reflecting the challenging weather conditions athletes have encountered in Glasgow.
Article Summary: Athletes advised to take preventive measures to minimise the risk of upper respiratory and airborne infections during the Commonwealth Games. A few Indian athletes have reported mild cold symptoms, including runny noses, but none has required hospitalisation. “It is quite cold and cloudy here,” Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra said.

Article Title: Ryan ten Doeschate returns to Knight Riders as Head of Cricket Strategy
Article Text:
Ryan Ten Doeschate (PTI Photo/Swapan Mahapatra)

Knight Riders Sports has appointed former Netherlands all-rounder Ryan ten Doeschate as its new Head of Cricket Strategy, bringing him back to the franchise where he enjoyed success as both a player and coach.In his new role, ten Doeschate will oversee cricket strategy, player scouting, recruitment, squad planning and talent development across the Knight Riders' global teams.He will also work as assistant coach for Trinbago Knight Riders in the CPL, Abu Dhabi Knight Riders in the ILT20 and Los Angeles Knight Riders in Major League Cricket.Knight Riders Sports CEO Venky Mysore welcomed the appointment, saying, “We are delighted to welcome Tendo back to the Knight Riders family. His deep understanding of our philosophy, combined with his experience across franchise and international cricket, makes him ideally suited for this role. He will help shape the next phase of growth across the Knight Riders ecosystem.”Ten Doeschate also expressed his excitement about returning, adding, “I'm excited to be back with the Knight Riders in this role. This is a unique opportunity to work with the coaching & analytics teams across our global franchises to strengthen our scouting/player development systems, and to build a long-term cricket strategy.”Ten Doeschate first joined Kolkata Knight Riders as a player in 2011 and was part of the IPL-winning teams in 2012 and 2014.He later returned as a coach in 2022 and played a key role in the franchise's third IPL title triumph in 2024.His latest appointment marks another chapter in his long association with the Knight Riders family.

Article Title: India turn to Saransh Jain for Sri Lanka Tests
Article Text:
Saransh Jain (BCCI Photo)

MUMBAI: Showing that age is no bar for selection, India’s national selection committee, led by former pacer Ajit Agarkar , on Tuesday handed a maiden call-up to Madhya Pradesh’s 33-year-old offspinning allrounder Saransh Jain for the two-Test series in Sri Lanka in August.As TOI reported on Monday (July 27), fast bowler Jasprit Bumrah and No. 3 batter Sai Sudharsan have been picked subject to fitness clearance from the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Bengaluru. Bumrah has been advised rest until July 30, after which he will report to the CoE. Ravindra Jadeja , who was rested along with Bumrah for the oneoff Test against Afghanistan and had been suffering from tennis elbow, has expectedly returned to the squad. Jadeja has been training in Rajkot in recent days, indicating that he had been asked to be ready for the Sri Lanka tour.Washington Sundar’s unavailability for the first Test due to the hamstring injury he sustained during the ODI series in England opened the door for Jain, the only new face in the squad.The presence of several lefthanders in Sri Lanka’s batting line-up also appears to have prompted the selectors to bring in the seasoned off-spinner.The BCCI also did not reveal the nature of Sudharsan’s injury. The left-hander was in excellent form on the recent India ‘A’ tour of Sri Lanka, scoring centuries in both four-day games.Should Sudharsan fail to clear his fitness test, Karnataka lefthander Devdutt Padikkal could slot in at No. 3. Left-arm spinner Manav Suthar, who took seven wickets on Test debut against Afghanistan, has retained his placeIndia squad for Sri Lanka Tests:Shubman Gill (capt), KL Rahul (vicecapt), Yashasvi Jaiswal, Rishabh Pant (wk), Sai Sudharsan*, Dhruv Jurel (wk), Ravindra Jadeja, Kuldeep Yadav, Manav Suthar, Jasprit Bumrah*, Mohammed Siraj, Prasidh Krishna, Gurnoor Brar, Devdutt Padikkal, Saransh Jain. *Subject to fitness clearance
